Nominal GDP stood at Rs 88.27 lakh crore, up 10.3 per cent from Rs 80 lakh crore in Q1 FY26.The RBI has projected India’s full-year GDP growth for FY27 at 6.7 per cent, up from its earlier forecast of 6.6 per cent.MoSPI is scheduled to release the next set of quarterly GDP estimates, covering July-September, on November 30.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: In 2012, a derelict 1866 Washington house was listed on a waterfront lot worth more without it; preservationists spent 6 years buying it and 8 more restoring it before reopening it in 2026
articles.summary: US News: In 2012, a crumbling 1866 farmhouse sat on a prized waterfront lot in Coupeville, Washington, listed for sale at a price that reflected the land’s val.
articles.body: In 2012, a crumbling 1866 farmhouse sat on a prized waterfront lot in Coupeville, Washington, listed for sale at a price that reflected the land’s value far more than the building’s. The Haller House, one of the oldest surviving structures on Whidbey Island, was in such poor condition that many assumed it would be demolished to make way for a new home. Instead, a group of local preservationists stepped in, spending six years raising funds and negotiating to save the house, then another eight years carefully restoring it. In 2026, the Haller House finally reopened to the public as a museum and community space, a testament to what can happen when a community decides a piece of its history is worth fighting for, according to updates and historical accounts from Historic Whidbey, the nonprofit that led the rescue and restoration.A house older than the state itselfThe Haller House was built in 1866 by early settlers on Whidbey Island, just a few years after the Civil War and three decades before Washington became a state. Originally a modest farmhouse, it grew over time as the family expanded, adding rooms and outbuildings that reflected changing needs and tastes.For more than a century, the house stood as a quiet witness to the island’s transformation: from logging and farming to tourism and commuter communities. But by the early 2000s, years of neglect, water damage and deferred maintenance had left the structure in serious trouble. Roofs leaked, foundations shifted, and parts of the framing were compromised. To many observers, the house looked like a lost cause.The moment it almost disappearedIn 2012, the Haller House and its waterfront lot came up for sale. The asking price was driven largely by the value of the land, with its views of Penn Cove and proximity to Coupeville’s historic downtown. From a purely financial perspective, it made more sense to tear down the house and build something new than to try to save it.For Historic Whidbey, a local preservation nonprofit, the listing was a warning bell. If the house was lost, one of the last tangible links to the island’s earliest Euro-American settlement would disappear. The organisation began exploring whether it could purchase the property, even though it lacked the funds at the time.Six years to secure the houseWhat followed was a long, uncertain campaign to raise money and build support. Historic Whidbey worked with donors, grant-making organisations and community members to piece together enough capital to buy the Haller House and its lot. The effort included: Fundraising events and membership drives; applications for state and private preservation grants; and outreach to residents who remembered the house from childhood or had family connections to it.In 2018, six years after the house first appeared on the market, Historic Whidbey finally completed the purchase. By then, the building had deteriorated further, and the real work was only beginning.Eight years of careful restorationRestoring the Haller House was not a simple renovation. The goal was to stabilise the structure, repair or replace damaged elements and return the house to a condition that reflected its historical character while making it safe and accessible for visitors.Key phases of the work included: Structural repairs to foundations, sills and framing to stop ongoing movement and decay; roof replacement and drainage improvements to prevent future water damage; careful removal of later additions and alterations that obscured the house’s original layout; restoration of historic windows, doors, mouldings and finishes using period-appropriate materials and techniques; and installation of modern systems—electrical, plumbing, heating and fire protection—in ways that minimised visual impact.Throughout the process, volunteers and staff documented the house’s construction phases, salvaged original materials where possible and consulted historical records to guide decisions. The work stretched over eight years, with progress sometimes slowed by funding gaps, weather and the sheer complexity of working with an aging, hand-built structure.Reopening in 2026 as a community resourceIn 2026, the Haller House finally reopened its doors. No longer a derelict eyesore or a private residence, it now serves as a museum and community space operated by Historic Whidbey. Visitors can tour the restored rooms, learn about the families who lived there and explore exhibits on Whidbey Island’s early history, from Indigenous use of the land to pioneer settlement and maritime industries.The house also hosts educational programs, lectures and special events that connect residents and visitors to the island’s heritage. For a community that has grown rapidly in recent decades, the Haller House offers a physical anchor to the past, a place where people can touch the same woodwork, walk the same floors and look out the same windows as those who built the community more than 150 years ago.Why this kind of preservation mattersThe Haller House story is unusual in its scale and timeline. Still, it reflects a broader truth about historic preservation: saving old buildings is often harder, slower and more expensive than it looks from the outside. It requires patience, sustained funding and a willingness to accept that some projects will take decades.For Whidbey Island, the payoff is a tangible link to its origins. In a region where many historic structures have been lost to fire, redevelopment or neglect, the Haller House stands as proof that communities can choose a different path. It also demonstrates how a single building can become a catalyst for broader interest in local history, inspiring people to learn more about the landscapes, industries and cultures that shaped the place they call home.A model for other small communitiesHistoric Whidbey’s approach, combining grassroots fundraising, professional restoration and long-term stewardship, offers a model for other small towns and rural areas facing similar choices. Not every old house can or should be saved, but when a building carries exceptional historical value and community support, projects like the Haller House show what is possible.Today, the house is more than a restored structure; it is a symbol of what a community can accomplish when it decides that its history is worth investing in. From a derelict 1866 farmhouse on a valuable waterfront lot to a reopened museum in 2026, the Haller House’s second life is a reminder that some stories are worth waiting for.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2015, Alibaba founder Jack Ma paid $23 million for 28,100 acres in New York’s Adirondacks; he planned to conserve its forests, trout streams and white-tailed deer habitat
articles.summary: US News: In 2015, Alibaba founder Jack Ma purchased the vast Brandon Park estate in New York's Adirondacks for $23 million, focusing on conservation to protect forests, trout streams, and wildlife habitats, while also serving as a personal retreat.
articles.body: In the summer of 2015, a tract of New York's Adirondack wilderness changed hands in a deal that drew attention far beyond the region. Jack Ma, the co-founder of Alibaba, had acquired Brandon Park, a vast private estate of forests, rivers, ponds and wildlife habitat. Unlike a conventional luxury property purchase, Ma's representatives said the land was bought principally for conservation, although he also planned to use it as an occasional retreat. The purchase put a large privately owned landscape under the control of an entrepreneur known for environmental interests in China. It also raised a broader question about the role private ownership can play in conserving landscapes that are valuable for forests, freshwater and wildlife.A vast forest beside the St Regis RiverAccording to the Adirondack Daily Enterprise, Jack Ma paid $23 million for the 28,100-acre Brandon Park estate in Franklin County, in the northwestern Adirondacks. The property included nearly 10 miles of the St. Regis River, trout streams, woodlands and several homes and guest cabins. Other reports on the purchase noted that the estate also contained lakes, ponds, a trout fishery, a horse barn and a maple-syrup operation. The land had a long conservation history before Ma acquired it. Much of Brandon Park had once formed part of a larger private preserve associated with William A. Rockefeller Jr. The Rockefeller family's Adirondack holdings reflected an era when wealthy industrialists established large private estates in the region, often combining hunting and fishing with forest management.By the time Ma bought Brandon Park, however, the property was already part of the larger Adirondack Park, a six-million-acre landscape made up of both public and private land. Ma's purchase did not turn the 28,100 acres into public Forest Preserve land. Instead, the property remained privately owned while its new owner said conservation would be its principal purpose. According to a study published in Landscape and Urban Planning, privately owned working forests and conservation lands form an important part of the Adirondack landscape, and areas perceived as wilderness are not necessarily publicly owned. The research found that some landscapes residents and visitors viewed as wilderness were actually privately managed forests, underscoring the role of private stewardship in preserving the region's undeveloped character.Forests, trout streams and wildlifeBrandon Park’s ecological value came from its forests and waterways. Contemporary reports described the property as containing extensive woodlands, trout waters and habitat for white-tailed deer. Its river frontage, streams, lakes and ponds formed a connected landscape supporting aquatic and terrestrial wildlife.According to research published in the Journal of Wildlife Management, white-tailed deer in the Adirondacks use specific wintering areas where features such as dense conifer cover and watercourses provide suitable conditions. The study highlights the importance of forest structure and landscape features to deer habitat, providing broader ecological context for the type of landscape found at Brandon Park. Rather, keeping a large property relatively undeveloped can help retain existing habitat and maintain ecological connections within a wider landscape.Conservation through private ownershipMa's stated intention was to preserve Brandon Park while retaining the option of using it as a personal retreat. His spokesman said a nonprofit entity would be established to manage the property and described the purchase as Ma's first investment in conservation land outside China.Later reporting in Adirondack Life said the property, then known as New Brandon, was being maintained by local employees and remained connected to Ma's conservation efforts. The magazine also reported Ma's involvement with other international conservation organisations, including the Paradise International Foundation. In that context, the significance of the purchase extends beyond its price to how the property was intended to be managed and conserved.In a region where private land makes up a substantial portion of the Adirondack landscape, the acquisition also illustrates how private ownership can influence the future of large, ecologically connected areas. For Ma, Brandon Park represented both a potential retreat and a conservation project. For the surrounding region, its value lies in the landscape itself: forests along rivers, streams and lakes that support aquatic life, and connected habitats used by wildlife.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: India's GDP growth: BJP hails 'economic resilience'; Congress asks where are the jobs?
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The BJP and Congress on Tuesday traded sharply contrasting assessments of India’s economy after official data showed GDP growth of 7.8 per .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP and Congress on Tuesday traded sharply contrasting assessments of India’s economy after official data showed GDP growth of 7.8 per cent in the April-June 2026 quarter. While the BJP hailed the performance as evidence of resilient economic management, the Opposition questioned whether the growth has translated into jobs, higher incomes and wider prosperity.BJP leader Ravi Shankar Prasad held a press conference where he described the latest growth figures as “particularly significant”. He argued that India had expanded rapidly despite heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty during the quarter, including the Gulf crisis, disruptions to oil supplies and supply-chain pressures.“Today is a very encouraging day. The latest report shows that India’s GDP growth stood at 7.8 per cent in the April-June 2026 quarter. The figure of 7.8 per cent is particularly significant because, during this period, the Gulf crisis had intensified. There were concerns over oil supplies, disruptions in supply chains, and uncertainty across the global economy. Despite all these challenges, India’s economy grew by 7.8 per cent,” Prasad said at a press conference in Delhi.Prasad also compared India’s performance with growth recorded by several other major economies, saying Canada grew by around 1.5 per cent, Germany by 1 per cent, the UK by 2.1 per cent, Malaysia by about 6 per cent, South Korea by around 3.7 per cent and the US by roughly 2 per cent during the same period.He attributed India’s performance to what he called effective economic management and praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s leadership.“Today, I would like to congratulate and commend India’s economic management. I also wholeheartedly congratulate the honourable Prime Minister for his vision, wisdom and leadership,” Prasad said.The Congress, however, challenged the BJP’s interpretation of the GDP figures, arguing that headline growth alone does not adequately capture the economic conditions faced by ordinary Indians.Congress leader Pawan Khera questioned how the 7.8 per cent growth figure was benefiting young people and farmers, while also pointing to concerns over employment, manufacturing, education and income distribution.“The Prime Minister comes up with a reel, a video. Ask him: the largest demographic in this country is the youth. How does this GDP growth affect the youth? How does it address the issues that young people face? The largest occupation in this country is agriculture. How does this GDP growth affect the agricultural sector? If it doesn’t benefit these two sectors, how does it affect the dwindling manufacturing sector? Look at the manufacturing data. So, what is he even talking about? A handful of people contribute to the growth of this country, but where is the redistribution of income? Where is the distribution of income? So, let’s talk about these fundamental issues. 80 per cent of this country depends on free ration. Is that what good GDP growth does for the country? That’s our question.”Khera had earlier taken his criticism to X, arguing that a single quarter of strong GDP growth should not be treated as evidence of broad-based economic prosperity.“One quarter of 7.8% growth is not an economic spring. If India has truly "bloomed," why do rampant unemployment, leaked exam papers, and a crumbling education system define the ground reality? Why is the republic's prosperity not translating into the prosperity of its public? GDP measures national output - not jobs, not wages, not opportunity. If it measured any of those, the future of India's youth would not look so bleak. Modi can manage his headlines. For India's youth, the question remains the same as ever: Where are the jobs?”At his press conference, Khera also questioned whether the strong GDP reading had resulted in tangible improvements in the cost of living and employment conditions.“On one hand, they say, "Look at the GDP of a single quarter and applaud." On the other, they say, "Don't buy gold, don't host lavish weddings." They themselves sit abroad while telling the country's citizens not to travel overseas and to save money. 80% of the population relies on free rations, but keep applauding... Regarding this 7.8% figure—what benefit is the country's largest sector, agriculture, deriving from it? The youth constitute the country's largest demographic; what benefit are they getting? Have their issues been resolved? Have milk prices dropped? Is there no longer a need for free rations? Have you rectified the employment situation to reverse the 45-year record low? Is manufacturing back on track? What happened to the MSME sector? What happened to the unorganized sector? If you have answers showing a positive outcome, then we, too, will applaud...”The competing responses underline the political divide over how India's economic performance should be assessed. While the BJP has used the 7.8 per cent quarterly expansion to highlight India's relative resilience amid global disruptions, the Congress has focused on whether headline GDP growth is being reflected in employment, household incomes and opportunities for India's young population.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Quote of the day by Princess Diana: "I like to be a free spirit. Some don't like that, but…" - powerful words on being yourself
articles.summary: UK News: Princess Diana's words reflect her genuinely independent nature and her willingness to remain true to herself, even when doing so clearly stood apart .
articles.body: Princess Diana's words reflect her genuinely independent nature and her willingness to remain true to herself, even when doing so clearly stood apart from what was expected of her public role. "I like to be a free spirit," she said. "Some don't like that, but that's the way I am." Diana became one of the most recognisable members of the British royal family, and her genuine popularity was closely connected to the way she presented herself as approachable and human, often following her own instincts rather than the formal expectations traditionally associated with royal life. Her words carry a genuinely simple message about being yourself, accepting real criticism, and having the confidence to live honestly according to your own actual personality, a lesson that showed up in her public life in ways considerably more visible than a single quote ever could.Quote of the day by Princess Diana"I like to be a free spirit. Some don't like that, but that's the way I am"A real moment that captured this exact ideaOne of the clearest real examples of Diana's independence came through fashion rather than words. In 1994, she wore a striking black off-the-shoulder dress designed by Christina Stambolian to a public event, on the very same evening that Prince Charles publicly admitted adultery on television. The dress became widely known afterwards as the "revenge dress," and it was understood at the time as a deliberate, quiet statement made entirely on her own terms, a genuinely visible way of showing the public that she remained confident and independent regardless of what was happening around her privately. That single evening captured something real about the personality behind today's quote, someone willing to be seen exactly as she actually was, rather than as anyone else expected her to present herself.The deeper meaning of Princess Diana’s quoteDiana's words suggest that she genuinely valued her own freedom to actually be herself, even at moments when other people clearly did not approve. Being a "free spirit" can mean having a genuinely independent personality, following your own instincts, and refusing to let other people's expectations completely determine how you behave. The second half of the quote matters just as much as the first. Diana acknowledges honestly that some people may genuinely dislike her nature, yet she never suggests that their disapproval should actually change who she is underneath it all.Why simply being yourself can genuinely be difficultBeing authentic sounds genuinely simple in theory, yet it becomes considerably harder once people are constantly watching or judging you, exactly as Diana experienced throughout her adult life. Real expectations from family, colleagues or wider society can influence how people actually behave, creating genuine pressure to fit in, avoid criticism, or behave in ways that simply make other people comfortable. Diana's quote suggests that real individuality sometimes requires honestly accepting that not everyone will ever genuinely approve of you.Princess Diana's public life faced genuinely intense scrutinyDiana entered the British royal family at a genuinely young age and quickly became one of the most photographed people in the entire world. Her clothing, her relationships and her personal life were frequently discussed across the media, and living under that level of attention made complete privacy almost impossible to maintain. Yet she developed a genuinely distinctive public personality regardless, often appearing considerably more relaxed and spontaneous than the formal image traditionally associated with royal life before her.How Diana actually expressed her individualityDiana became known specifically for the way she interacted directly with people. She was often photographed speaking closely with members of the public during her charitable work, famously abandoning the formal royal protocol of wearing gloves so she could actually touch the people she met. Her approach helped create a genuine image of a royal figure willing to step outside traditional convention, and that individuality became a genuine part of her lasting public appeal.Being genuinely independent never actually meant ignoring everyone elseBeing a free spirit does not necessarily mean refusing all advice or simply doing whatever you want regardless of consequence. Healthy independence involves making your own real decisions while still genuinely understanding that other people may hold different opinions. Diana's quote recognises this reality honestly. She knew that some people would never actually approve of her personality, yet she remained comfortable enough with herself not to let every single piece of criticism determine her actual behaviour.Why fear of criticism can genuinely make people hide their true personalityA real fear of judgement can encourage people to quietly change themselves purely to fit outside expectation. Someone might avoid expressing a genuine opinion or pursuing a real interest simply because they are worried about how others will actually react to it. Over time, constantly seeking outside approval can make it genuinely difficult to even know what you actually want anymore. Diana's words offer a genuinely different approach instead, accepting honestly that criticism exists without letting it completely control your own identity.The real importance of accepting that not everyone will like youTrying to be liked by absolutely everyone is genuinely impossible. Different people hold different values, personalities and real expectations, and a decision that one person genuinely admires may frustrate someone else entirely. Accepting this honestly can make it considerably easier to actually live with real confidence, while also spending considerably less energy trying to satisfy every single outside opinion that comes your way.Other memorable quotes by Princess Diana"When you are happy you can forgive a great deal.""I don't go by the rule book… I lead from the heart, not the head.""Anywhere I see suffering, that is where I want to be, doing what I can.""If you find someone you love in your life, then hang on to that love."How to embrace Princess Diana's lessonKnow yourself genuinely, understanding your own values, interests and personality honestly.Accept real disagreement, since someone disliking your choices does not automatically mean they are actually right.Do not live entirely for outside approval, since constantly seeking validation can make you lose sight of what you genuinely want.Stay open to genuinely useful criticism, since being independent has never actually meant refusing to learn.Make your own real decisions, taking honest responsibility for the choices that actually shape your life.Protect your own individuality, remembering you never actually have to copy everyone around you.Be genuinely comfortable being different, since standing apart can sometimes become a real strength.Set healthy boundaries, respecting other people's opinions without letting them actually control you.Follow your real interests, giving yourself genuine permission to explore what actually matters to you.Stay authentic, letting your actions honestly reflect who you actually are underneath it all.Why Princess Diana's quote remains relevantDiana's words capture a genuine tension that a great many people experience, the desire to be themselves while also genuinely wanting to be accepted by others around them. Her message was never that criticism should always be ignored entirely. It suggests instead that a person's real identity should never be completely shaped by other people's approval alone. Being yourself can sometimes genuinely mean disappointing people, challenging outside expectation, or choosing a path that others simply do not understand. Diana's own description of herself as a "free spirit" reflects that genuine willingness to remain individual despite real outside judgement. You cannot actually control whether everyone genuinely likes who you are. You can, however, genuinely choose whether their opinions ultimately determine who you become.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: About 20 years ago, Dawn Robinson paid $40,000 for 2.4 acres in New Jersey; Middle Township later offered her $47,000 and is now trying to take the land for a 340-home project
articles.summary: US News: In South Jersey's Middle Township, a war goes on. The township has filed an eminent domain condemnation complaint that seeks to acquire 2.4 acres of l.
articles.body: In South Jersey's Middle Township, a war goes on. The township has filed an eminent domain condemnation complaint that seeks to acquire 2.4 acres of land in Whitesboro for a large-scale housing development project. But the woman who owns the property, Dawn Robinson, does not want to give it up, according to a report by WHYY.“The land is already paid for,” Robinson said. “If I wanted to sell, I would have had a ‘for sale’ sign on it. I’m not being rude, I don’t want to sell. I want to keep it for my kids.”An eminent domainWhat does eminent domain mean? Well, an eminent domain gives the government the power to take away someone's private property. However, the Fifth Amendment states a property may only be taken away if it is for public use and the owner is paid just compensation.Middle Township wants to take her land in order to move forward with a multi-million dollar housing development plan, known as the Indian Trail Redevelopment project, to be built by a private, for-profit developer, NVR, Inc, also known as Ryan Homes. A show-cause hearing on the matter that was scheduled for May 6 was postponed until July 1. At a second court appearance in July, Robinson agreed to attend a mediation session to try to negotiate a land-swap settlement, but no deal was reached during the closed-door session, so the case could soon head back to court.Robinson hopes to convince a judge the housing development plan on the table doesn’t need to include her property. “I would love to keep my land and develop it myself,” she said. “I bought this land from the township, they didn’t tell me there was an expiration on it.”“They could build around me, no problem,” she added. She stressed that her property is on the outer edge of where the developer wants to build the housing project.Robinson shared that nine years ago, an attempt was made to force the acquisition of dozens of parcels of land using eminent domain, but a judge rejected the proposal and the redevelopment of the area stalled.Kerrin Wolf, an associate law professor at Stockton University, said that if a town uses eminent domain, there needs to be a specific plan in place to redevelop the area in question. “They use [eminent domain] sometimes to build schools, sometimes to expand roadways, sometimes for public-private partnerships,” Wolf said.Eminent domain can be used for commercial developments, as long as officials can prove the project is for legitimate public use. “They have to show that the development will be good for the community in some significant way, you have to have a very specific plan that shows clear public good,” he said.“Eminent domain is supposed to be for public use,” said Robinson. “Everyone knows that is not happening in this case.” She pointed out that last month the New Jersey Supreme Court issued a unanimous decision in Jackson Township v. Getzel Bee. In that case, the court ruled that local governments cannot use eminent domain to condemn private land and then transfer it to a developer.Affordable housing on the other sideMiddle Township Mayor Christopher Leusner has strongly supported efforts to move the project forward, calling it “a transformative initiative” that will bolster township services. He said in a statement that the 340-home project “will deliver much-needed housing, help fulfil the township’s affordable housing obligations, generate millions in new revenue for the township and convert long-vacant, fragmented land into a vibrant residential community.”James Maley, a partner at the law firm Maley Givens in Collingswood, said his firm will represent Middle Township in the condemnation proceeding. He said the lots being taken are extremely small and were given to people in the 1930s as part of a newspaper promotion.“The township has been working for 10 years on assembling lots so that [the property] can be developed,” Maley said. “A development of this nature is critical for the community to provide more opportunities for decent housing. It will also increase the [township’s] ratable base and make the township more affordable for everyone.”Maley said affordable housing units will be offered as part of the project, and that dozens of lots have already been acquired in preparation for the development to move forward.Help from outsideRobinson's friend, Janice Roots, helped convince the co-founders of Truth and Record, an online platform that advocates for social justice and accountability, to help spread the word about her case and collect donations for her legal defence. “They work on behalf of the descendants of those sold as enslaved people,” Roots said. “They have a strong network throughout the country, and I felt they would be a good resource.”Roots said she felt compelled to help Robinson for personal reasons. “My family has been through the exact same situation,” she said. “My great-great-grandfather received 40 acres after emancipation around 1870. Subsequently, the land was seized from him, and I didn’t want to see history repeat itself with Dawn.”Rachel Davis, the co-founder of Truth and Record said they decided to help Robinson since they felt it was an "unjust case." “Eminent domain is often used by the government to displace predominantly Black and Brown people and poor people, and our stories that we tell come from that historical perspective.”Truth and Record’s other co-founder Chelsea Nicolas said the case raises several red flags. “This case is located in a historically Black neighbourhood, and eminent domain is being used to seize land for a private developer, she said. “The significance of this on economic security, inheritance, community continuity, all of those things are impacted.”She said a website has been established to help collect donations for Robinson’s legal costs and to tell her story. Robinson said she feels honoured that people in her community and others she doesn’t even know are helping her.“I think my neighbours believe that if it happens to me, it can happen to them, with eminent domain, that they can just take your ownership from you if they want your land,” she said.Robinson said even if she wanted to sell, part of the legal agreement she has been offered stipulates that if the land ever needs to be remediated, she would be financially responsible for whatever needed to be done, even after the sale was complete. “If they find anything on it, tomorrow or 20 years from now, I’m responsible for that,” Robinson said. “How can they take something from me and hold me responsible?”Robinson said she has been offered $47,000 for her 2.4-acre property, which is right next to her current home. However, that is only $7,000 more than what she initially paid for the property 23 years ago. She said she originally owned two lots, but that the township split one of them in half, so technically, she is now the owner of three parcels of land.If an agreement is not reached, the case will head back to Superior Court at an unspecified date for a final judgment on whether the township has the authority to take Robinson’s property. If the eminent domain complaint is upheld, a three-person commission would then decide the value of her 2.4 acres.“I’m not in the way,” she said. “I really can’t say they need [my property], I feel it’s more that they just want it.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Massive chemical fire erupts at electrical transformer plant in Mississippi, forcing evacuation
articles.summary: A paint booth fire near an explosive tanker truck triggered a massive blaze at Howard Industries in Laurel, Mississippi, forcing evacuations.
articles.body: Flames and thick black smoke billowed from a manufacturing facility in Mississippi on Monday as a massive chemical fire forced employees to evacuate and drew fire crews from across the county, according to local reports. The fire broke out at a Howard Industries facility in Laurel after a paint booth caught fire next to a tanker truck carrying an explosive substance, Mayor Johnny Magee told local media. All employees were evacuated, and fire departments across Jones County were called to the scene, according to WDAM-TV. Crews had mostly contained the fire by 8 p.m. SHOCKING VIDEO SHOWS GIANT BLACK PLUME OF SMOKE RISING FROM TENNESSEE PLASTIC RECYCLING FACILITY FIRE Video posted to social media showed flames burning at the facility as thick smoke filled the sky and fire trucks arrived. Several loud booms could be heard as people ran from the area and firefighters worked near the fire, according to WAPT-TV. "Everybody’s gotta leave," Brandon Herford Brewer, who posted one of the videos, could be heard saying. Brewer described the heat as unbearable as he prepared to leave the area. "My face is melting," he said. "It’s Howard industry, and I’m about to get out of here. I am sweating down." EMERGENCY CREWS RESPONDING TO MASSIVE EXPLOSION AT NEW ORLEANS-AREA OIL REFINERY: SHERIFF Brewer later said the building had been cleared and everyone had gotten out. Howard Industries makes electrical transformers, including the equipment utilities use to get electricity to homes and businesses. The company says its Laurel plant covers about 2.3 million square feet. Officials urged people to avoid the area, warning that traffic could slow firefighters and put workers and first responders at risk. It was not immediately clear whether anyone was injured or how much damage the fire caused. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Officials did not immediately release more information.

articles.title: Northampton's Alan Carr immortalised in street art festival
articles.summary: James Thompson says more than 360 artists contributed to the three-day street art event.
articles.body:
Northampton's Alan Carr has been immortalised in a mural as part of one of Europe's largest street art events.

From Saturday 29 August to Monday 31 August the town became a "living canvas" as more than 360 artists came together to paint over walls and buildings that were earmarked as needing improvement and to cover illegal graffiti.

Wall Games was founded by artist James Thompson in the hopes of bringing more people to the town and leaving a lasting legacy.

He said: "It's a legacy we are trying to leave here to create a street art trail and a tour that doesn't just last for the weekend, but lasts for a longer period and gives people a reason to come and visit the town."

The festival and celebration of live art has become a key event in the town's calendar after previously taking place between 2020 and 2022. And with so much artwork scattered across the town, Thompson said it would take hours to see it all.

With support from West Northamptonshire Council and Northampton BID it has grown from a grassroots community project into a nationally recognised event.

Thompson said: "There's some amazing walls out there. I've seen some fantastic walls on Giles Street where there's some local artists that have done some incredible artwork. My personal favourite is Smug One, he's painted a large picture of a male in a baseball cap and a hoodie on the side of the old Corn Exchange building near Mayorhold car park.

"For me, being a Northampton resident and loving the town as I do, trying to find creative ways to bring people to the town and explore areas that perhaps they weren't aware of and didn't know about is important to me."

articles.title: Ukraine war: What to make of Modi's plea to Putin to end conflict
articles.summary: BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at why the Indian PM made a very public peace plea to his Russian ally.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has been urged by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a close ally, to end Moscow's war against Ukraine.

"Every day spent in war pushes humanity back, and every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm," Modi said on Monday.

Modi, whose country's economy depends heavily on discounted oil from Moscow, has made several similar pleas to Putin since he launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at what lies behind Modi's renewed appeal for peace, and Putin's response.

Modi's comments on ending the war in Ukraine are not surprising and don't suggest any tactical change in India's foreign policy.

In fact, speaking on the sidelines of a regional summit in 2022 - less than a year into the conflict - Modi told Putin publicly that "now is not the time for war".

But it would be an oversimplification to suggest that Modi's current or past statements on the war can be seen as a rebuff to Putin or Russia's strategy.

Western countries have pushed Modi hard to take a clear stand on the war - but Delhi has largely stayed neutral, urging dialogue to end the war instead.

The stand hasn't made many Western capitals happy but they have continued to court Modi and India - it's just too big and too fast-growing an economy to be ignored.

In this context, Modi's current statement cannot be seen as an attempt to please a third country.

If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?

The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.

Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.

Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.

But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.

Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.

So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.

As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.

This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.

Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.

There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.

To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:

"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."

After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.

All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.

Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.

Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.

And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

In recent days Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine.

"After [Russia] intensified its strikes on Ukraine's military-industrial facilities and critical infrastructure," wrote the Kommersant newspaper this morning, "the Russian side is convinced that in the military confrontation time is working against Kyiv."

While Putin believes that, he'll be reluctant to pause his so-called "special military operation".

articles.title: Social media photo craze sparks tourist invasion at picture-perfect vacation hot spot
articles.summary: Videos show long lines forming at Santorini's blue-domed churches in Oia as tourists line up in the early morning for iconic travel photos seen on social media.
articles.body: Long lines of tourists are forming at some of Santorini's most famous photo spots as visitors seek out the island's iconic views. Videos circulating online show crowds lining the narrow streets of Oia to pose in front of the Greek island's famous blue-domed churches — with some visitors lining up early in the morning for their turn. Mandee Migliaccio, CEO of New Jersey-based Stepping Out Travel, told Fox News Digital that Santorini was a bucket-list destination long before social media, but she believes that today's platforms have amplified travelers' desire to capture the same iconic images. ONCE-GLAMOROUS VACATION SPOT OVERRUN BY INFLUENCERS AND CROWDS: 'ALMOST UNBEARABLE' "People are wanting to go get those iconic pictures," Migliaccio said. "It's been there, but yes, it has been amplified." The churches, with their brightly colored domes, are among the island's most photographed locations — along with sunsets, windmills and whitewashed staircases, she said. Crowding can become particularly intense when cruise ships are in port. "You have thousands upon thousands of people getting off the boats and wanting to take the same four pictures," Migliaccio said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER She encouraged travelers not to plan their entire experience around recreating photos they've seen online. "Make your own story. Make your own vacation," she said. "Don't just go there and plan a trip around four photos you're gonna take [on the trip]." For those who still want the famous shots, she recommended going early and staying several days. On Mondays and Tuesdays, there tend to be more cruise ships in port, while Sundays may be less crowded, she said. The scenes have also sparked discussion online about whether social media has been changing the way people travel. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES "Traveling is so much fun if you're not doing it for social media," one TikTok user commented. Reddit users have expressed mixed views as well. One commenter said seeing the same destinations online repeatedly can create expectations and diminish some of the surprise, while also acknowledging that social media has made planning trips easier. Another person called social media "an amazing resource" for discovering places, restaurants and attractions they otherwise might have missed. Migliaccio said travelers can also use social media to highlight experiences beyond the same famous photo spots, including cooking classes, wine tours and other parts of the island. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "Santorini is so beautiful and there's so much to do," she said. "And it's not just about the photos. Go experience it." She also urged visitors to remember that the island is home to local residents. articles.title: Pakistan wins Indus waters battle at The Hague, but India threat remains
articles.summary: The Permanent Court of Arbitration says the treaty remains binding. But India has rejected the findings.
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan – A court of arbitration in The Hague has ruled that India cannot unilaterally suspend the Indus Waters Treaty , rejecting every argument New Delhi has used to justify holding the six-decade-old water-sharing agreement “in abeyance” since April 2025.

In a unanimous decision issued on Monday, the five-member court found that the treaty “remains fully in force” and that India “must observe its obligations” under it, including those governing the design and operation of hydropower projects on rivers that flow into Pakistan.

The ruling is the first time an international court has ruled on whether India’s decision to place the treaty in abeyance is legally valid.

India announced the decision in April 2025, after a deadly attack on tourists in Indian-administered Kashmir, saying it would suspend the treaty until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ends support for cross-border terrorism. Islamabad denies accusations that it was behind the attack, in which 26 civilians were killed by gunmen who first tried to determine the religion of their victims.

India has rejected the jurisdiction of the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) – an intergovernmental court outside the United Nations system whose mandate New Delhi has accepted in other cases – in the Indus Waters Treaty case brought by Pakistan to The Hague. India did not participate in any of the hearings that culminated in Monday’s ruling.

It was quick to reject the verdict, leaving Pakistan with a legal and diplomatic victory whose actual worth will now be tested.

After India placed the treaty in abeyance in April 2025, Pakistan applied in March 2026 for the PCA to rule on the treaty’s status, arguing it could not order India to comply with an agreement that might no longer be in force.

The court invited India to take part, but India did not respond. Hearings went ahead at the Peace Palace in The Hague from April 26 to 28, 2026, with only Pakistan present.

The court examined every ground India has cited publicly: Sovereignty, Pakistan’s alleged unwillingness to renegotiate, cross-border terrorism, and changes such as demographic growth, clean-energy needs and climate change.

The court rejected all of them, finding that no rule of international law allows a state to unilaterally suspend a treaty on the grounds that it was a sovereign nation within its rights to walk away from a pact.

Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar welcomed the ruling.

“Pakistan welcomes the unanimous Award of the Court of Arbitration today, which decisively rejects India’s unlawful attempt to place the Indus Waters Treaty ‘in abeyance’ and reaffirms that the Treaty remains fully in force and binding on both parties,” he said in a statement on X. “India must fully comply with its obligations under the Treaty and with the binding decisions of its dispute settlement mechanisms.”

India, for its part, rejected the ruling within hours.

In a statement, India’s Ministry of External Affairs called the court “illegally constituted”.

Abeyance, it said, “remains in force” until Pakistan “credibly and irrevocably” ends support for cross-border attacks, a charge Islamabad denies.

Legal experts say the ruling strengthens Pakistan’s position, even if it offers no obvious way to force India’s hand.

“This is not merely declaratory,” Ahmer Bilal Soofi, an international law expert who also served as Pakistan’s caretaker federal law minister, told Al Jazeera. “It gives Pakistan a very categorical, clear legal basis to consider countermeasures under international law, whenever it chooses to do so.”

Sikander Ahmed Shah, professor of international law at the Lahore University of Management Sciences, agreed that India’s absence from the hearings does not weaken the outcome.

“India’s non-participation doesn’t make any difference. The court has established that it has jurisdiction, and India signed the treaty,” he told Al Jazeera. “This is a PCA judgement, and its value and precedent under international law carry real weight.”

Both, however, acknowledged that there is no formal enforcement mechanism comparable to a UN Security Council order.

Pakistani officials have already set out what compliance would look like in practice.

At an international seminar on the treaty in Islamabad on June 30, Pakistan’s Indus Waters commissioner, Syed Mehar Ali Shah, called for “an immediate Commission meeting, general and special tours and inspections”.

The Permanent Indus Commission, the joint body of Pakistani and Indian officials set up to run the treaty day-to-day, has not met since May 2022.

Pakistan says India has also stopped sharing routine river-flow data and blocked site inspections since 2023, both of which the treaty requires.

Dar made a similar case in Washington on August 28, calling on both countries to “resume and strengthen the process of technical dialogue, transparency, and data sharing”.

The deputy prime minister made the remarks virtually, addressing a separate seminar on the treaty hosted by Pakistan’s embassy in Washington, three days before Monday’s ruling.

Beyond that, Soofi said, Pakistan’s options narrow to diplomatic pressure exerted at international forums.

Since India’s unilateral decision to walk away from the Indus Waters pact, Pakistani officials and military leaders have increasingly described the dispute in existential terms.

Commissioner Shah, at the June 30 seminar, called flow predictability “part of the survival architecture of the state”.

Federal Minister for Climate Change Musadik Malik, at the same event, called the dispute “a crisis of justice”, not simply one of water or climate.

Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, chairman of the Pakistan Peoples Party and a former foreign minister, told the same June 30 seminar that the dispute was “not a technical dispute … not a matter of paperwork, hydrology, or administrative abeyance. This is the weaponisation of water.”

He asked: “How can Pakistan be expected to sustain a ceasefire when India continues to pose an existential threat?”

A few weeks later, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif went further still.

Addressing the inauguration of a war memorial in Islamabad on August 13, flanked by the army, navy and air force chiefs, a day before Pakistan’s Independence Day, he declared, “every single drop of Pakistan’s water is our red line.”

He warned India would face “a crushing response with even greater force” than the May 2025 conflict if it moved against Pakistan’s water or sovereignty, according to the state-run Associated Press of Pakistan.

Hassan Abbas, an Islamabad-based hydrology and water resources expert, disagreed with the suggestion, however, that the breakdown of the pact for the moment posed an imminent threat to Pakistan.

“I don’t think there is an existential threat as such right now,” he told Al Jazeera. “The western rivers are protected by geography, not primarily by the treaty.”

India’s built storage capacity on the Chenab River is roughly 1 million acre-ft (405,000 hectare-ft), he noted, small next to Pakistan’s own seasonal irrigation needs.

“If they say they won’t let water flow, they will end up flooding themselves,” he said, since the Indian dams are run-of-river hydropower plants with little storage room.

“Once their dams are full, they have no option but to let water go,” Abbas added.

But he was also critical of Pakistan’s own water management.

Islamabad’s fixation on new mega-dams, he argued, ignores cheaper fixes. Raising irrigation efficiency could free up more water than new reservoirs will ever store, the water expert said.

articles.title: Daily barrages of intense storms threaten flooding, damage in the Northeast … again
articles.summary: Another stormy stretch is underway in the Northeast, renewing flooding and storm damage concerns for a region that’s endured several bouts in recent weeks.
articles.body: Another stormy stretch is underway in the Northeast, renewing flooding and storm damage concerns for a region that’s endured several bouts in recent weeks. ⛈️ Get your local forecast in the CNN Weather app ☔️ Repetitive rounds of rain and storms with little reprieve between them each day began on Sunday and will continue through at least Thursday. A heat dome is partially responsible: It’s steering the jet stream — the river of air storms flow through — into the region as it bakes areas farther south with record-challenging heat. It’s not just rain that’s concerning for the Northeast. Severe thunderstorms are expected Tuesday through Thursday that could deliver damaging wind gusts, hail and even a few tornadoes. Here’s what to expect each day. Tuesday’s forecast A few rounds of scattered severe thunderstorms are possible Tuesday. Showers and thunderstorms moved through parts of New England, New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania in the morning. These storms weren’t severe, but some will continue into the afternoon and could cause isolated flooding issues. A new round of severe thunderstorms is possible starting late in the afternoon or early in the evening around southern New York. These storms will likely push south and east into Tuesday night. Damaging wind gusts are the main threat with any severe thunderstorms, but some hail and a couple of tornadoes are also possible. Any storm, severe or not, could also deliver heavy rain. Flooding issues should be isolated, but any area caught under multiple storms is at the greatest risk for street flooding or rises on smaller waterways. Wednesday’s forecast The forecast is basically a rinse and repeat of Tuesday’s, but the afternoon severe thunderstorm threat is shaping up to be a bit more concerning. Strong to severe thunderstorms are possible in the morning, especially near the eastern Great Lakes. These early storms will eventually diminish and give the atmosphere enough time to recharge for another round starting in the afternoon. Storms may still be scattered, but there could also be a few supercell thunderstorms. Supercells are more likely to bring stronger winds, drop larger hail and produce longer-lived tornadoes than other types of storms. Some non-supercell storms could also congeal into more organized lines of storms that would increase the threat of wind damage. Wednesday’s flood threat is also higher than Tuesday’s because the storms could be stronger and move over the same areas rained on in previous days. Thursday’s forecast Rain and storm threats will start to shift away from the Northeast on Thursday, but isolated flooding issues are still possible in much of southern New England and parts of eastern New York — including New York City — New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Stronger storms with damaging winds and hail will focus mainly on the Mid-Atlantic, including Washington, DC. Parts of southern Pennsylvania and southern New Jersey could still get clipped by these storms. The best chance for these damaging storms is from later in the afternoon into Thursday night. The Northeast will mostly dry out on Friday and remain that way through the weekend.

articles.title: Endangered kakapo parrot population reaches 325 in New Zealand after record baby boom
articles.summary: There’s been a baby boom among one of the world’s most endangered parrot species - and it’s something to crow about.
articles.body: There’s been a baby boom among one of the world’s most endangered parrot species — and officials in New Zealand are squawking about it. A record 90 chicks have been added to the count of the endangered kakapo parrot, bringing the population to a record 325 birds, the New Zealand Conservation Department said in a statement Tuesday. The fledglings of the bird, which is native to New Zealand, were bred this year. The youngest is now 150 days old, a milestone at which the baby birds are considered independent enough to be added to the tally. And every bird counts. The green parrots do not fly and have a waddling gait, making them an easy target for ground predators. The kakapo is also the heaviest parrot species, with males weighing up to 9 pounds. The bright birds, with finely blotched yellow-green plumage and large gray beaks, are also thought to be among the longest‑living bird species, reaching 60–90 years, the statement from the department said. The nocturnal parrots with their owl-like faces remain critically endangered, conservationists say. “There is still a long road of recovery ahead, but ninety chicks in a single season is a record. In the early years of recovery, it took 16 years to produce that many chicks,” said Deidre Vercoe, manager of the department’s kakapo recovery operations. “We had a four-year gap between breeding seasons, so it’s fantastic to finally see the population increase,” she said in a statement. “It’s also a significant milestone for the species, as the last time the population is thought to have exceeded 300 birds may have been as long as 75 years ago.” The Kakapo Recovery Programme began in 1995 with a population of just 51 birds, including only 20 females. Since then, the species has been through 13 breeding seasons, with recovery efforts working to overcome challenges associated with low genetic diversity, including infertility and poor hatching success. The successful season also highlights the importance of creating more predator-free habitats for the species. Each kakapo in the program is fitted with a small backpack radio transmitter to help track its location and monitor its activity levels, conservationists say. Once widespread across New Zealand, kakapo numbers plummeted after human arrival due to hunting, predators and habitat loss. Conservation efforts began in 1894 but the species nearly went extinct by the mid‑1900s. The bird is believed to have lost the ability to fly as it evolved because there were no ground level predators in the New Zealand environment to threaten the species. But human colonization several hundred years ago introduced predators such as cats and rats that wiped out most of the kakapo. Today, surviving kakapos are kept on small protected offshore islands. They largely live off berries from native Rimu trees, which bear fruit every two to four years, impacting their mating and slow repopulation. A representative on the kakapo recovery group, Tāne Davis, said the measure of success isn’t just in the numbers. This season, the program trialed “several approaches aimed at reducing intensive management, such as fewer egg and chick checks through careful monitoring of remote nest technology data, and reducing supplementary feeding,” Tāne said. “Our focus is increasingly on determining where intensive intervention is still needed and where we can start to return to more natural levels of kakapo breeding outcomes.” For many of this year’s chicks, the next milestone will be receiving a name on the anniversary of their hatch days next year. However, a small number of 2026 chicks will remain unnamed to signify the gradual shift toward a more natural future for the species as it continues its recovery journey, the group said. Early predictions suggest there may not be such a long wait between breeding seasons, Vercoe added. The group’s modeling “indicates there may be only a two-year gap between breeding seasons this time round. So, while we’ll take a moment to stop and reflect on this remarkable year, we’re already looking ahead to 2028 and preparing for what could come next,” she said.

articles.title: Children go underground as Ukraine starts new school year under constant Russian fire
articles.summary: As children arrived at the Ukrainian Global School in Kyiv for the start of a new school year on Tuesday, they went straight to the basement.
articles.body: As children arrived at the Ukrainian Global School in Kyiv for the start of a new school year on Tuesday, they went straight to the basement. Given the near-constant Russian attacks on the capital over the past few days, the school decided it was no longer sustainable for the students to go down to the underground shelters whenever an air raid siren rang. Instead, they will have their classes there. “This is a significant change,” the school told parents and guardians in a letter marking the start of the new academic year. “Now, during an air raid alert, there’s no need to run anywhere, interrupt classes, or wait for hours to resume learning. The children are already where it’s safe. And school simply continues.” In an effort to lighten the tone given the grim situation facing students and their families, the letter framed the move as taking school “to a whole new level.” Russia has been pummelling Kyiv with what is now the longest, most intense aerial attack against the capital – just as Ukrainian families prepare for the start of the new school year. According to a CNN tally, air raid alerts went off 60 times in Kyiv between midnight on Thursday and noon on Tuesday, lasting around 47 hours in total. According to local authorities, at least 53 people have been killed and more than 100 injured in Kyiv and the Kyiv region during that time. Russia has been bombing Ukrainian cities since the opening salvos of the full-scale war in February 2022, but its campaign of aerial terror against Ukrainian civilians intensified at the beginning of last year, when Moscow became capable of mass-producing the Iranian-designed Shahed drones. Moscow used to launch these massive attacks mostly overnight, when it was easier to avoid Ukrainian air defenses. But in recent months, it has been attacking continuously, day and night, using its new-generation jet-powered drones. Three times faster than the original Shaheds, these drones are nearly impossible for Ukraine to intercept. Lost generation Few of the Ukrainian children headed back to school on Tuesday could remember what school was like before the war. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine just as the world began to emerge from the Covid-19 pandemic, which means that children starting eighth grade on Tuesday are the youngest Ukrainians to have experienced normal, uninterrupted schooling. Those headed to the fifth grade or younger have never been to school during peacetime. Kyiv authorities told parents to prepare for the possibility of attacks disturbing school and urged them to teach their children what to do during an alert. “In the current circumstances, this is just as much a part of preparing for the new school year as packing a school bag or getting the school uniform ready,” the Kyiv City office said. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky visited a school in Kyiv to mark the start of the new academic year. Dressed in their Sunday best, the boys in button-down shirts and the girls wearing traditional ribbons in their hair, the children were excited to see the president – even though their meeting took place in a shelter instead of a classroom because of yet another air alarm. “There is an air raid alert right now. Unfortunately, the Russians are despicable … even among enemies, there is usually an understanding that children are children,” Zelensky told reporters. Empty seats As the war stretches into the fifth school year, its horrific toll on communities becomes increasingly tangible. With more than 1.8 million children now living abroad according to UNICEF and many more displaced within Ukraine, the number of empty seats is rising in classrooms across the country. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Education, schools across the country welcomed some 243,398 first-graders on Tuesday, far fewer than the 400,000 who started school in 2021, before the war started. Nadiia Andrianova, whose nine-year-old daughter Aiia started third grade on Tuesday, is among those who decided to relocate. She said she felt the situation has worsened to the point where she couldn’t handle it any more. She said she noticed a significant deterioration in the security situation in Kyiv in the spring of 2025, but decided to stay put. “But the whole of last academic year was very difficult, especially at night. We usually go to sleep in the underground (the Kyiv Metro), as it’s the safest shelter available in our city. And these nights spent in the underground have simply become very frequent. It takes me several days after such a night to recover and function normally,” she told CNN. When Russian ballistic missile attacks became more frequent, she gave up. “Every Kyiv resident knows that you simply don’t have time to find cover – you can’t run anywhere in those few minutes. It’s just a matter of luck. So I decided to look for another city, another place to live.” Aiia started a new school in western Ukraine on Tuesday – a move she was initially very opposed to. “She didn’t want to go because she had a brilliant school there (in Kyiv), with excellent teachers … she’s been playing the piano for two years, she has friends there, and her best friend stayed in Kyiv, so, of course, she didn’t want to go,” Andrianova said, adding that Aiia finally agreed to the move after one particularly harrowing night in Kyiv. “We were woken up by horrific explosions and sat in the corridor of our flat because we hadn’t had time to run anywhere, just listening to the explosions every 20 seconds. And we agreed that we would leave, that we would stay in Ukraine, but move to a safer city.”

articles.title: How wildfires are scorching France’s wine industry
articles.summary: Europe’s largest wine exporter is already battling a cocktail of crisis from heatwaves to lower sales.
articles.body:
As wildfires razed swaths of Western Europe this summer, wineries in the region have grown increasingly concerned about the fate of one of the area’s most important exports.

In France, Europe’s largest wine exporter by far, some 739,000 hectares (1.8 million acres) of land is dedicated to vineyards that sprawl across wine-making regions such as Languedoc, Bordeaux and the Rhone Valley. So has it been for centuries.

But now, human-induced climate change is causing more extreme weather conditions, threatening the precious and fragile grapes, which are particularly sensitive to heat. Worse, the frequency of wildfires in the tinder-dry forests is rising, causing havoc to agriculture.

This year, Western Europe endured one of its hottest summers, aggravated by the El Nino weather phenomenon, which is characterised by hotter, drier conditions. Europe is now the planet’s fastest-warming continent, and in some places, is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather.

This year’s hot season began with a suffocating heat dome in May, and by mid-August, punishing temperatures reached 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) in some areas. Wildfires tore through areas of Gironde, southwestern France, close to Bordeaux and in the heart of wine country.

Higher temperatures force grapes to ripen much faster than normal. While that produces a more sugary flavour, it also affects the grape’s natural acidity and pushes up alcohol content in the wine it produces.

With forests tinder-dry, destructive wildfires have also broken out at a scale never recorded before, including in wine country.

Where have wildfires occurred in France?

The 2026 wildfire season in southwest Europe has been one of the worst in decades, with a series of huge blazes recorded in France between June and July.

At least 465,000 hectares (115,000 acres) of land have been burned since the start of the year, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told reporters amid the inferno in July.

In the southwest Gironde region alone, an area about four times the size of Paris was burned in the largest fire there since 1949. The department’s capital is Bordeaux, one of the country’s most important wine-growing regions and home to many iconic French wines.

Authorities launched a massive evacuation effort, with some 220,000 people needing to leave their homes, including those living close to Bordeaux, as the blazes engulfed the Gironde’s vast pine forests. The fires were so intense that they created lightning bolts and ignited even more flames.

Southwestern Landes, Var, as well as areas in the Aude and Herault regions have also been affected.

By September 1, some small fires were still active in the south, including in Saumos, about an hour from Bordeaux, according to the monitoring website Feux de forets . All of the blazes are now under control.

Although the fires reached within 15 kilometres (9 miles) of Bordeaux, most of the region’s vineyards, which are located further inland, have been largely untouched, Per Karlsson, a wine expert who runs a wine tour agency, BK Wine Tours, alongside his wife, told Al Jazeera.

However, some growers are at risk not from the fires, but from the smoke. That’s because the wind can carry smoke and ash much farther than the fires themselves reach. In July, as the fires were raging, Al Jazeera’s Nina Montagu-Smith reported ash falling on the wine-region town of Libourne, more than 100km (62 miles) from the source of the fires on Cap Ferret, a narrow peninsula on France’s Atlantic coast, west of Bordeaux. Libourne is close to the important wine centre of Saint-Emilion.

“When I visited Arcachon, a seaside town just across the bay from Cap Ferret, we could see the fires on the peninsula. Within hours, the sky had blackened, and the smoke was thick over Arcachon town,” Montagu-Smith said.

The spreading smoke “may have caused a bit of ‘smoke taint’”, Karlsson explained.

Smoke can damage grapes by penetrating their skin and releasing a smoky flavour during fermentation. That affects the taste and aroma, and lowers the overall quality of the juice and resulting wine. Rinsing the grapes when absorption has already occurred does little to help, he added.

Another issue is that wine tourism has been affected. Wineries view tourism as a significant additional source of revenue at a time when wine consumption is falling generally.

“Wine tourism is becoming a very important aspect of the industry,” Karlsson said. He and his wife organise private tasting trips to vineyards, including in Bordeaux and other parts of France.

“Large numbers of wineries in Bordeaux are open to it these days, although it used to be very hard to get into them,” he said.

Amid the wildfires, tourists are worried about venturing into some areas, he added. In late July, as the Gironde wildfire raged, the French government also appealed to the public to avoid the region.

What other challenges are winemakers facing?

Besides the wildfires and scorching heat, an ongoing drought in Western Europe is also affecting grape growers.

Critical water sources such as the Danube River and the Rhine have retreated drastically, affecting producers in several countries.

In eastern France, the Doubs River has all but vanished in some places, revealing parched riverbeds. Authorities have been forced to enforce water-use restrictions in many areas. In July, France’s Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut said at a crisis meeting that this year’s drought was “exceptional” in its intensity, and had occurred despite average rainfall.

Grape-growing regions traditionally depend on rainfall because authorities have banned irrigation to force vines to seek groundwater naturally. The main reason for this was to ensure higher quality, as unregulated irrigation can cause grapes to absorb too much water, bloating the fruit and diluting the flavour of wine.

But vines need sufficient water to produce big, juicy berries. During droughts, when vines don’t get adequate water, they draw it from the grapes instead, causing the berries to shrink, experts say.

Stephane Vignon, a winemaker in the village of Verzenay, northeastern France, told Reuters that some bunches of grapes weighed nearly 30 percent less than their typical weight this year.

The combined crises brought the harvest season in France forward to August this year, much earlier than the traditional September harvest time, as farmers feared losses from accelerated ripening and reduced acidity.

Compounding this, the wine industry in France is facing weaker sales due to shifting habits, as globally, people are drinking less wine.

In the United States, the world’s largest wine-drinking country and France’s biggest buyer, wine consumption went from 3.3 billion litres (872 million gallons) in 2020 to 2.7 billion litres (717 million gallons) in 2024, according to the California-based Wine Institute.

US President Donald Trump’s tariffs on French wine in 2025, and repeated threats to hike the taxes, have not helped declining sales.

“Climate change for the foreseeable future is manageable,” Karlsson noted, pointing out that grape growers are starting to adapt their farming behaviours by planting more tolerant grape varieties, for example. But fewer wine drinkers? “That’s the bigger issue,” he concluded.

articles.title: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, takes over from Tim Cook after 15 years
articles.summary: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus takes the helm of the iconic tech giant on Tuesday, ending Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure during which the company’s value skyrocket to $4.6 trillion thanks to the iPhone’s enormous popularity.
articles.body: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus takes the helm of the iconic tech giant on Tuesday, ending Tim Cook’s 15-year tenure during which the company’s value skyrocket to $4.6 trillion thanks to the iPhone’s enormous popularity. The transition to a new CEO comes at a pivotal time for Apple. Artificial intelligence has unleashed the greatest upheaval within the industry since Steve Jobs unveiled the first iPhone in 2007. Apple has gotten off to a rough start in AI after stumbling in its efforts to deliver new features built on the technology, as promised nearly two years ago. Earlier this year, it unveiled new artificial intelligence advances, including upgrades to its Siri assistant, emphasizing a focus on privacy and day-to-day use as the iPhone maker tries to catch up with rivals. Ternus faces challenges that will force him to step outside his comfort zone in hardware engineering. Beyond finding ways to keep Apple competitive in the artificial intelligence race, he will need to navigate supply chain questions and relationships with figures such as President Donald Trump, who offered public praise for his predecessor on Tuesday. Serving as Apple CEO will also require soft skills, including developing relationships with important figures. Cook cultivated ties with Trump as he navigated the company through business challenges, including Trump’s trade and tariff war targeting countries in Asia, where Apple has extensive manufacturing supply chains. Although he is handing over the CEO reins at Apple, Cook is widely expected to help the company maintain a good relationship with Trump after he shifts to his new role as executive chairman. Ternus worked on some of Apple’s signature products under Cook, including the Apple Watch, AirPods and Apple Vision Pro. He will headline next week’s launch of the latest iPhone at Apple’s Cupertino, California, headquarters.
