articles.title: Europe blasts Russian finance minister’s attendance at Asheville G20
articles.summary: European financial officials pushed back on the U.S. decision to invite Russia’s finance minister to the G20 finance meeting in Asheville, N.C., this week. The European officials expressed concern that the Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov’s presence at the summit of the world’s 20 largest economies risked normalizing ties with Moscow amid its full-scale war…
articles.body:
European financial officials pushed back on the U.S. decision to invite Russia’s finance minister to the G20 finance meeting in Asheville, N.C., this week.

The European officials expressed concern that the Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov’s presence at the summit of the world’s 20 largest economies risked normalizing ties with Moscow amid its full-scale war against Ukraine.

July marked the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians amid increased Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks, as well as Ukraine’s shortage of air defense munitions. Fighting over the winter is also expected to intensify suffering in Ukraine.

Russia’s Finance Ministry said that Siluanov met with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the two discussed the Russian-American financial relationship and issues of cooperation within the G20.

A source familiar told The Hill that Bessent “made clear” to Siluanov that the U.S. “will not provide Russia with economic relief until the war in Ukraine is over.”

“When he tried to discuss areas of interest to take action on, Secretary Bessent forcefully interrupted and said nothing is possible until the war is over,” the source said.

The meeting comes as Congress is debating a new sanctions bill targeting Russia. The legislation would give the president power to tariff the top five countries purchasing Russian oil, among other measures.

However, President Trump has downplayed and threatened U.S. support for Ukraine since returning to the White House in an attempt to mediate with Moscow. When Russia stalled talks to end the war, Trump imposed sanctions on major Russian oil companies, Lukoil and Rosneft, in October 2025.

But German Finance ⁠Minister Lars Klingbeil told reporters at the summit he worried about the message the U.S. was sending to Russia by inviting its officials to the G20 meeting, and that Europe was readying another package of sanctions against Moscow.

“A joint approach would ​be best, yet it is sometimes unclear whether there might be a loosening of the stance over there. That is why I find the signal sent by receiving the Russian finance minister ​here quite troubling,” Klingbeil said, Reuters reported .

“I would have wanted greater clarity from ​the American side that he should not be received here as a normal guest.”

European ministers and central bankers also opposed appearing in the normal “family photo” of participants, Reuters reported, and that in the end a decision was made to take the photograph without the Russian minister.

The U.S, as host of the G20, makes up the guest list and excluded South Africa , last year’s G20 host. The Trump administration has accused Pretoria of persecuting White South Africans, charges the government denies , and created a special refugee program giving them priority access to resettle in the U.S.

Spain was also absent from the G20 meeting. President Trump has lashed out against Madrid for refusing to pledge to increase its defense spending to five percent of its GDP and pushed back against Spain’s criticism of the U.S. and Israeli war in Iran.

articles.title: A WWII-era training plane was packed into boxes in 1953; its owner carried the pieces through 3 moves for 50 years before the forgotten aircraft was finally restored
articles.summary: US News: A World War II-era training aircraft  that spent nearly five decades packed away in boxes after its retirement, moving with its private owner from one.
articles.body: A World War II-era training aircraft that spent nearly five decades packed away in boxes after its retirement, moving with its private owner from one place to another, has now been restored to airworthy condition.The WACO UPF-7, serial number 5650, began its training role in 1941, Vintage Aviation News reported. It was purchased by Unger Aircraft Association through the Civilian Pilot Training Program (CPTP), a government-backed programme created to help train pilots before and during World War II. The aircraft later also helped train pilots connected with the Korean War era.In 1953, the WACO was retired and bought by a private owner in Florida. Instead of being scrapped, the aircraft was taken apart and packed into boxes. The owner planned to restore it himself one day, but that restoration did not happen for decades.The aircraft remained in storage as its owner moved three times over a period of 50 years, carrying the boxed-up parts with him. In 2002, a pilot rediscovered the aircraft in the owner's storage unit while acquiring a Piper aircraft from him on behalf of RARE Aircraft Ltd. of Faribault, Minnesota. This changed the story of the aircraft.The WACO UPF-7The WACO UPF-7 was built between 1937 and 1942 as a primary trainer. It had a combination of wood, steel and fabric construction, along with an open cockpit. Depending on the aircraft, the type could be fitted with a Jacobs or Continental engine and a Hamilton propeller.Its design made it suitable for people learning the basics of flying. The aircraft was considered easy to manoeuvre and stable, qualities that were important for primary pilot training. It is estimated that 50% of World War II pilots received their initial training in a WACO UPF-7.The aircraft's history was linked to the wider development of WACO. The company that became known as the Weaver Aircraft Company was started by George E Weaver, Clayton Bruckner and Elwood 'Sam' Junkin in Troy, Ohio, in 1920.According to the report, by 1929, the company was known as Waco Aircraft Company. During the 1930s, it built and sold more aircraft than all other US commercial aircraft companies combined. By the time the company left aircraft production in 1947, it had produced 62 different aircraft models that were operated in 35 countries.How WACO ended up in storageThe UPF-7 was among the aircraft used in the CPTP. At the time, the US government wanted to support pilot training for college students while the country was still following an isolationist policy at the beginning of World War II.Civilian Fixed Base Operators, or FBOs, such as Unger, purchased aircraft for the programme. They could then recover their investment through federally funded training programmes such as CPTP. These arrangements also included yearly hangar leases for $1.After the UPF-7 was retired in 1953, its private owner in Florida chose to preserve it rather than dispose of it. The aircraft was dismantled and placed into boxes with the intention of carrying out a restoration at some point.That decision meant the aircraft survived, but it also left it forgotten for many years. The owner carried the boxes through three moves over the next five decades before the aircraft was rediscovered in 2002.RARE Aircraft then took on the restoration. Much of the aircraft's steel framework was retained, while a large portion of the wood was replaced.Restoration after decades The original aircraft had a Grade A cotton covering. During the restoration, much of this was replaced with Dacron, which is now a standard material used in aircraft restoration.The restoration also preserved some of the aircraft's original components in unexpected ways. The original wing ribbing was later used as a conference room table at the museum where the aircraft was displayed.The aircraft's registration also required a change. Its original registration number, N32019, had been used on another aircraft. RARE Aircraft therefore obtained N32018 from the US Federal Aviation Administration for the restored WACO.After restoration, the aircraft was fitted with a Jacobs R75582M engine and a Hamilton Standard constant-speed propeller. It became airworthy and was displayed at the Historic Flight Foundation.Photographs by aviation historian and writer Randy Malmstrom show the restored aircraft, including its two open cockpits, instrument panel, landing gear and Jacobs R-755 engine.The aircraft was displayed at the Historic Flight Foundation when the museum was located at Paine Field in Everett/Mukilteo, Washington. The foundation later moved to Spokane.The aircraft's time with the Historic Flight Foundation eventually came to an end. After the dissolution of the foundation, the WACO UPF-7 was sold to a private owner in Lakeland, Florida.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Times Square stabbing victim identified as 32-year-old banker from New Jersey
articles.summary: A 32-year-old Bank of America vice president was killed Monday afternoon after authorities say an emotionally disturbed woman started stabbing people in the heart of Times Square.
articles.body: A 32-year-old Bank of America vice president was killed Monday afternoon after authorities say an emotionally disturbed woman started stabbing people in the heart of Times Square. Erin Piacenti, from Chester, New Jersey, was stabbed in the abdomen, according to the New York Police Department. She was pronounced dead at a hospital a short time after the attack in the tourist-heavy area near 41st Street and Seventh Avenue. Bank of America confirmed Piacenti was a vice president within Business Selection and Conflicts in Global Corporate and Investment Banking. “We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed,” the bank said in a statement. “Our hearts go out to her family and all of her loved ones.” Piacenti’s cousin, Katie Guiltinan, told NBC News on Tuesday that she hopes more attention is focused on Piacenti than on the suspect. “It’s unbelievable,” a tearful Guiltinan, 35, said. “She was wonderful.” Police say Pamela Cisneros, the 49-year-old Queens woman shot dead by police after killing Piacenti and stabbing a 68-year-old man during the afternoon spree, had a documented history of mental health concerns. A witness told police that Cisneros took out the knives from a red Target bag before approaching the couple. After waving the weapons around, the suspect stabbed the 68-year-old man, who had just come out of the subway with his wife, in his side. She then went up a block and attacked Piacenti. The stabbings happened about 20 seconds apart. They are believed to be random and unprovoked, with no apparent connection to organized terrorism, according to law enforcement sources. The male victim was taken to Bellevue Hospital, where police said Tuesday he is in stable condition. “Tonight, our thoughts are, of course, with the victims of this horrific attack and their families. One life cut far too short by a senseless act of violence,” said Tisch. Following the two stabbings, Cisneros continued up Seventh Avenue, where she encountered police between 42nd and 43rd streets, police said. She was still armed with both knives at that time. Officers spoke to her for four minutes, telling her to drop the knives, but she refused, police said. The responding officers fired stun guns at her, which did not appear to be effective, police said. Cisneros then advanced toward the officers, two of whom opened fire at her. She was taken to the hospital, where she died. The NYPD had a documented history of mental health concerns regarding Cisneros dating back to 2018 and 2019, but she had no criminal history, Tisch said. Both knives allegedly used by the suspect were recovered at the scene.

articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: An unexpected roadside interaction between Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay and an elderly woman became one of the notable moments .
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An unexpected roadside interaction between Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay and an elderly woman became one of the notable moments of his visit to Mettur in Salem district on Tuesday. During the brief encounter, Vijay gifted the woman his own pair of Christian Dior sunglasses.Vijay was in Salem to open the gates of the Mettur Dam and release water for Samba cultivation in the Cauvery Delta. News agency PTI reported that after inspecting the Mettur hydroelectric power station and opening the sluice gates of the Stanley Reservoir, he made an unscheduled stop at a roadside farm while travelling towards Salem airport.According to local accounts, Vijay noticed a group of elderly women working in the fields and stepped out of his vehicle to meet them.Chellam, an elderly resident of the area, walked towards the chief minister and held his hand.“He asked me if I had eaten,” Chellam recalled. “I told him I hadn't, because I was waiting to see him first.”During the interaction, Vijay asked her name and enquired about her well-being before walking with her around the garden and the nearby cattle shed belonging to local farmer Palanisamy.Chellam said the chief minister then offered her the sunglasses he was carrying. I told him how happy I was to see him, and he gifted me these sunglasses,” she told PTI.According to Chellam, Vijay’s gesture reminded her of his days in cinema.“He looked just like he does in his movies,” she said. “I was so happy I told him I would defend him if anyone ever tried to harm him.”The chief minister spent around 15 minutes at the farm, during which he distributed dhotis and sarees to the host family and discussed local agricultural issues, including the government’s decision to increase the milk procurement price to Rs 44.Chellam later said Vijay also urged her to have food. “He told me he had already eaten and insisted that I go and eat,” she said.Videos of the interaction were subsequently shared widely on social media. articles.title: Judge to decide whether Tyler Robinson will stand trial in Charlie Kirk’s assassination
articles.summary: A judge in Utah is expected to decide whether there is enough evidence to move forward with a trial against the man accused of fatally shooting Charlie Kirk.
articles.body: A judge in Utah is expected to decide Tuesday whether there is enough evidence to move forward with a trial against Tyler Robinson, the 23-year-old man accused of fatally shooting prominent conservative political activist Charlie Kirk. Prosecutors have charged Robinson with aggravated murder, a first-degree felony that makes him eligible for the death penalty. Robinson has not yet entered a plea. Robinson turned himself in a day after Kirk was shot dead at an event at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10 last year. The assassination of Kirk, the 31-year-old co-founder of the youth advocacy group Turning Point USA and a close ally of President Donald Trump, rocked U.S. politics. District Judge Tony Graf has said lawyers on both sides of the case will have a maximum of two hours each to present closing arguments Tuesday before the court takes a one-hour break. Graf is expected to issue a ruling from the bench. Tuesday’s high-stakes hearing comes nearly two months after prosecutors laid out a detailed public reconstruction of the alleged events surrounding Kirk’s killing and presented a trove of evidence against Robinson, including surveillance footage, digital records and forensic material. David Hull, a former State Bureau of Investigation agent, characterized Robinson’s alleged movements before and after the assassination. Hull’s testimony amid a five-day hearing was accompanied by excerpts from campus surveillance footage shown in court for the first time. Robinson arrived at the university hours before the shooting, bought a meal from a campus Chick-fil-A restaurant, and made contact with representatives for Turning Point USA, Hull testified. Robinson then changed outfits and took position on a rooftop overlooking the amphitheater where Kirk was speaking, Hull said. In a video shown in court July 7, Robinson could be seen crouching down on the rooftop, Hull told the court. Then, after a bullet hit Kirk, Robinson could be seen darting across the roof, dropping to ground level and sprinting away on foot, the former investigator added. Prosecutors played another video featuring partially redacted excerpts from law enforcement investigators’ interview with Lance Twiggs, Robinson’s former romantic partner and roommate. The day after Kirk’s assassination, Twiggs told investigators, Robinson nervously paced their apartment and expressed regret. Twiggs told investigators that he asked Robinson whether it was true that he fatally shot Kirk. In the emotional interaction that followed, according to Twiggs, Robinson “said he wishes he hadn’t done it.” Twiggs told investigators that Robinson said he intended to confess to his parents or go to the police. He ultimately turned himself in to law enforcement authorities later that day. Investigators have said they found the suspected murder weapon — a bolt-action rifle — wrapped in a towel in a wooded area near the Utah Valley University amphitheater. DNA from both Robinson and Twiggs was on the towel, Sgt. Jennifer Faumuina of the Utah Department of Public Safety testified July 7. Robinson’s lawyers attempted to throw doubt on the DNA evidence and pressed a defense witness, FBI forensic analyst Amanda Bakker, on the potential for error in forensic testing and other issues. Robinson’s defense lawyers have not provided an alternative theory for who killed Kirk. In a charging document filed last September, prosecutors highlighted inscriptions allegedly etched on each round of the rifle, including the phrases “Hey Fascist! Catch!” and “If you Read This, You are GAY.” Twiggs, in the recorded interview played in court, told investigators that Robinson never talked about Kirk before the shooting. The roommates-turned-partners had originally bonded over their shared love of playing video games, Twiggs said.

articles.title: Trump has asked Apple to change Lake Ontario name: Burgum
articles.summary: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said that President Trump has asked tech company Apple to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” after an executive order from the president that pushed the name change. “I know that the president reached out to Apple directly, so I’m sure that we may be seeing that change…
articles.body:
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said that President Trump has asked tech company Apple to change the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” after an executive order from the president that pushed the name change.

“I know that the president reached out to Apple directly, so I’m sure that we may be seeing that change coming up soon to Lake America,” Burgum said Monday on Fox Business Network’s “Mornings with Maria” to the channel’s Cheryl Casone.

Apple Maps still showed Lake Ontario with its original name as of Tuesday morning.

Last week, Trump signed an executive order formally changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid recent trade tensions with Canada.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump said last Thursday.

In the last few weeks, Washington and Ottawa have been locked in a trade dispute, with both sides slapping tariffs on each others’ goods.

On Saturday, Google Maps changed the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” for users in the U.S., kept the original name for Canadian Google users, and kept both names for international users.

Google cited the Great Lake’s name switch-up to the U.S. Geographic Names Information System’s (GNIS) formal renaming.

“Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the U.S., people using Maps in the U.S. will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the U.S. and Canada will see both names,” the company said in a statement.

articles.title: France targets Shein and Temu with fast fashion fees
articles.summary: The levy on "ultra-fast fashion" items could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030.
articles.body:
France has started imposing fees on fast fashion items which could reach almost €20 per garment by 2030, as the government tries to curb sales of cheap clothing sold by e-commerce sites.

The levy, which came into force on Tuesday, follows a new law passed in June to regulate so-called "ultra-fast fashion" companies such as Shein, Temu and AliExpress.

The e-commerce giants, known for selling large volumes of cheap apparel, have been criticised by French officials for driving a surge in fast fashion.

China's commerce ministry has described the French law as discriminatory and a trade barrier, saying it could violate World Trade Organization (WTO) principles.

French minister Mathieu Lefevre said the "harmful effects of ultra-fast fashion" on the environment and economy were "well known".

In July, Lefevre's office said the levy would not apply to retailers such as H&M or Zara, prompting some to say that the measure appeared to spare European companies.

Under the legislation, ultra-fast fashion will be determined according to two factors: the volume of clothing placed on the market and the cost of repairing garments relative to their purchase price.

The per-item fee will vary on a set scale according to how each product scores on both these standards.

For 2026, the charges range from a €0.50 (£0.43) levy on underwear to €2 (£1.71) for T-shirts, to €9 (£7.71) for jeans and €12 (£10.28) for a jacket.

The levy could reach up to €19.50 (£16.71/$22.60) per item by 2030, though the cap remains at 50% of the product's pre-tax price.

The fees come after Shein, a fast fashion retailer founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, was valued at $26.2bn (£19.3bn) on its first day of public trading on the stock market in Hong Kong.

The company was once estimated to be worth nearly $100bn, but has faced heated competition, trade tensions and questions over the ethics of its supply chain.

The BBC has contacted Shein, Temu and AliExpress with a request to comment.

Shein previously told the BBC that the impact of legislation targeting ultra-fast fashion would "worsen the purchasing power of French consumers, at a time when they are already feeling the impact of the cost-of-living crisis".

Temu, a Chinese-owned e-commerce company, has also been widely criticised by politicians in the UK and US alike.

A spokesperson for Temu previously told the BBC that the brand "acknowledges the important environmental concerns addressed by the proposed French legislation", and argued that it does not operate as a fast fashion company because it is a marketplace and does not manufacture its own products.

articles.body:
Progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) quipped Monday that a company should build an AI data center near President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort, after he said communities will be “backwards and poor” if they oppose the construction of such facilities.

“How about we put one in Mar-a-Lago? I love that. Let’s put a data center up in Mar-a-Lago, we’ll see how backwards and poor he is in response to that,” Ocasio-Cortez told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez on Capitol Hill.

The president said Monday that communities pushing back on AI data centers will face negative economic consequences, saying the “only reason” they would not want the facilities “is if they want to end up being backwards and poor.”

Trump wrote on Truth Social , “If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them.”

Cloud South operates a data center less than 2 miles from Mar-a-Lago, located in Palm Beach, Fla. Last month, Palm Beach County commissioners voted against the development of another AI data center in the area, requiring the “Project Tango” team to resubmit its proposal.

Early in his second term, the president framed the AI race as one the country must win over China. But administration officials have in recent months acknowledged potential safety risks of new models.

A survey Fox News conducted last month found 70 percent of respondents opposed the construction of an AI data center in their area. That included 6 in 10 Republicans and more than three-fourths of Democrats.

Trump said Monday that China “could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement” in the U.S., adding Chinese leaders “can’t believe it is happening!”

GOP Rep. Tim Burchett (Tenn.) pushed back against the president’s remarks on Monday, telling Manríquez, “I guess I’m backwards and poor,”

The Tennessee Republican said, “We need more local control. We should have brought everybody to the table,” adding companies could build data centers in military installations instead of communities.

Trump has given Republican candidates wiggle room on AI , saying last month that “some people feel differently” on the issue .

“I’m only saying that if I ran a community … if I was a mayor or if I was a governor in the state, I would want to have the data centers because they bring tremendous income,” he told reporters.

articles.title: GIANNO CALDWELL: Sanctuary cities call it compassion. Patricia Fox calls it the ultimate price
articles.summary: Patricia Fox testified how sanctuary policies left daughter Carissa Aspnes minimally conscious while Colorado Medicaid denied her in-home nursing care.
articles.body: This week, Patricia Fox stood before the House Judiciary Committee’s Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement Subcommittee and told lawmakers what sanctuary policies actually cost a family. "My daughter, Carissa, was hit on March 28, 2025, by an illegal alien," she testified. "She was launched head first into a concrete barrier. The driver and passengers of the vehicle fled. Never checking to see if my daughter was alive." She continued: "Despite her initial prognosis, Carissa survived. Praise God. But survived and recovered are not the same." Sanctuary city and sanctuary state policies have been championed from coast to coast as the most compassionate, resolute action a city or state can take. But, no one has really asked what they cost the citizens who actually live there. Patricia Fox paid the ultimate price for sanctuary policies in Colorado. GRIEVING MOTHERS SCORCH DEM LAWMAKER AFTER HE PIVOTS DURING HEARING TO ATTACK 'MAGA REPUBLICANS' Carissa Aspnes was 22 years old and celebrating a new start. She had just returned home to Aurora, Colorado, from Chicago to launch a career as an esthetician, and on March 28, 2025, she climbed onto the back of a motorcycle to mark her birthday. Minutes later, an illegal immigrant from Venezuela, Valeria De Los Angeles Bermudez Marcano, ran a stop sign, crossed three lanes of traffic and slammed into the motorcycle. She and her passengers fled the scene, leaving Carissa unconscious on the road without checking whether she was alive. Carissa survived. However, 18 months later, her mother is still living what survival actually looks like. Carissa underwent emergency surgery to remove part of her skull and relieve brain swelling. She is now minimally conscious, nonverbal, wheelchair-bound and fed through a G-tube. "Every morning, I use a Hoyer lift to raise my adult daughter out of bed because she can’t sit up, stand or get herself up," Patricia testified. EXCLUSIVE: DHS HONORS ANGEL FAMILIES DURING NATIONAL CRIME VICTIMS WEEK, CALLS CRIMES 'COMPLETELY PREVENTABLE' Carissa's physician says she needs two people to safely assist her. "Colorado Medicaid denied us in-home nursing," Patricia said. "So I figure it out." Medicaid denied the wheelchair Carissa actually needs, too. So Patricia blends her daughter’s food, feeds her through the tube, brushes her teeth, bathes her and administers her medications, all while learning to read pain in a daughter who can no longer tell her where it hurts. The financial toll is staggering. Between emergency surgery, rehabilitation and the $3,000 to $4,000 a month in ongoing therapy, equipment, and care that insurance routinely denies, Patricia says Carissa’s medical bills already total seven figures. She has been trying to raise money to cover those expenses through a GoFundMe campaign. And the toll isn’t only financial. Patricia’s 19-year-old daughter has already begun preparing for the day she and her older brother must take over Carissa’s care. At 19, her future has been rewritten by a crash she had nothing to do with. DHS BLASTS CALIFORNIA SANCTUARY POLICIES AFTER JAIL RELEASES ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ACCUSED IN HIT-AND-RUN "One collision created an entire family of victims," Patricia testified. And justice never arrived. Prosecutors dropped every charge against Bermudez Marcano except a single reduced Class 5 felony. As part of the plea deal, she was ordered to pay $15,000 in restitution, but only for the motorcycle. For Carissa’s brain injury, her wheelchair, her feeding tube, her family’s shattered future, there was nothing. "A motorcycle received more justice than my daughter," Patricia testified. EXCLUSIVE: ANGEL DAD FINDS ‘NEW PURPOSE’ WITH ICE AFTER DAUGHTER’S KILLING TURNED HIS WORLD UPSIDE DOWN Bermudez Marcano was eventually deported, but only after Patricia’s family reached out directly to ICE’s Victims of Immigration Crime Engagement (VOICE) office, which was created to connect victims and their families with case updates, resources and support as they navigate the immigration enforcement process against the person who harmed them. Meanwhile, Colorado projected roughly $127 million from its General Fund this year for a program called Cover All Coloradans, which provides healthcare to people who lack qualifying immigration status, Patricia told the committee. Those are a state’s fiscal priorities laid bare: money for healthcare coverage regardless of legal status, while a citizen who was maimed by someone with no legal right to be driving on Colorado’s roads fights her own state’s Medicaid program for basic nursing care. OPEN BORDERS WERE INSANE, BUT POLITICIANS DIDN’T CARE. FAMILIES LIKE MINE PAID THE PRICE Patricia Fox is not a political operative. She is a mother who has become fluent in her daughter’s facial expressions, movements and heart rate because that’s the only language Carissa has left. Yet she made the trip to Washington anyway, sharing her family’s story as one of the Angel Families whose lives were permanently altered by policies that hand driving privileges to people who have no legal right to be behind the wheel in the first place. Carissa’s story is not isolated. Mary Ann Mendoza has spent over a decade fighting the same fight since an illegal immigrant driving the wrong way on an Arizona highway, three times over the legal limit, killed her son, Police Sgt. Brandon Mendoza, in 2014. Joe Abraham buried his 20-year-old daughter, Katie, after a previously deported illegal immigrant struck her car at nearly 80 miles per hour and fled the scene. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Roughly 19 states and Washington, D.C., now allow people to obtain a driver’s license regardless of immigration status, sometimes without requiring English proficiency to read a stop sign. This is not compassion. It is a public safety failure with a body count, and the families paying for it are the ones who did everything right. I started the Caldwell Institute for Public Safety and the Caldwell Foundation for Public Safety because I believe the safety of American citizens has to come before politics, on both sides of the aisle. Carissa Fox’s family should not have to choose between fighting Colorado Medicaid and fighting for their daughter’s dignity. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Every family in this piece did everything right. They followed the law, raised their children to do the same and still buried them or, in Patricia’s case, watched a daughter’s future disappear in an instant. Sanctuary policies didn’t protect Carissa, Brandon, or Katie. They protected the people who took everything from them. Until we stop calling that compassion, more families will learn the same lesson the hard way.

articles.title: Fairness for growers is food security for America
articles.summary: Rep. Vern Buchanan is calling on the Trump administration to implement seasonal tariff-rate quotas on Mexican produce during the ongoing USMCA review to protect Florida’s agricultural sector.
articles.body:
Food security begins at home. That’s why the ongoing review of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement is such an important moment for American agriculture, and for our country. During this review, the United States faces a clear choice: protect our ability to grow our own food or continue down a path of greater dependence on foreign food supplies, at the expense of our food security, our supply chains and Americans’ confidence in what’s on their plate.

As vice chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, I helped negotiate the agreement back in 2019 as the top Republican on the Trade Subcommittee, and even then, I pushed for accommodations for our seasonal growers. Today, the stakes for Florida are higher than ever. Agriculture is a cornerstone of our state’s economy, and the outcome of this review will help determine whether our Florida growers can keep producing the fruits and vegetables our country depends on.

For more than two decades, Mexican shippers have squeezed Florida farmers out of their own market by flooding it with low-priced produce during Florida’s own growing season. According to an October 2025 report from the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Florida’s share of the fruit and vegetable market has fallen by nearly 50 percent over the last two decades, while Mexico’s share has surged by more than 200 percent.

Bell peppers, cucumbers, squash, blueberries — entire sectors of Florida agriculture have taken steep losses in market share and revenue, even as consumer demand keeps growing. Multi-generational Florida farms, family operations that have fed this country for generations, are being forced to shut down.

Since the trade agreement with Mexico and Canada took effect, the volume of these disruptive imports has only accelerated, jumping from $14 billion in 2020 to roughly $19 billion today. That surge has widened our already large agricultural trade deficit with Mexico and pushed more Florida growers to the breaking point.

The Trump administration recognizes this problem. Unchecked seasonal import volumes from Mexico are putting Florida agriculture at risk, and the administration is right to make finding a solution a priority in this review of teh agreement.

The solution Florida’s industry has put forward is pragmatic, measured and long overdue: seasonal, product-specific tariff-rate quotas on Mexican produce during Florida’s marketing season. Such quotas are a well-established, targeted trade tool already used across American agriculture. They strike the right balance, keeping trade flowing while preventing the seasonal surges that undercut a stable domestic supply. Any new agreement with Mexico should include this approach so we don’t further compromise Florida’s ability to grow food at home.

Florida is not alone. Fruit and vegetable growers well beyond our state are facing the same pressures as import volumes surge, and they have joined Florida in calling for a real solution. We agree: our trade agreements should never come at the expense of American agriculture’s survival.

Earlier this year, I authored a bipartisan letter to President Trump , alongside Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Fla.) and members of the Florida delegation, urging his administration to address the harm caused by these unchecked seasonal import surges. That call is even more urgent today.

At current rates, we risk permanently losing production capacity in key fruit and vegetable sectors. Once our farms, our infrastructure and generations of agricultural know-how are gone in favor of foreign production, they may never come back.

This review of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement gives our country a real opportunity to restore fairness for our seasonal produce growers, strengthen our food security and build a food system Americans can rely on and trust. For the sake of Florida’s growers and for a food supply this country can always count on, now is the time to act.

Vern Buchanan represents Florida’s 16th District in the U.S. House of representatives and serves as vice chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack on Leipzig airport
articles.summary: Germany has accused Russia of being involved in the foiled drone attack targeting a busy airport in Leipzig last month, the country’s interior minister said Tuesday.
articles.body: Germany has accused Russia of being responsible for the drone attack targeting Leipzig airport last month and announced a slew of new measures against Moscow. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid attacks,” Germany’s interior minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters, as he raised the country’s threat level assessment from “general” to “high”. Germany’s foreign minister Johann Wadephul also ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn, and the Russian House, a cultural center, in Berlin. Germany is also tightening controls Russians entrying the country. The US previously assessed that an explosive-laden drone discovered at the airport in east Germany belonged to a Russian intelligence service, a US defense official in Europe told CNN. The incident caused major disruptions and sparked security concerns across Europe. According to German authorities at the time, the drone was discovered inside a secure area of the Leipzig/Halle Airport on August 5 near the airport’s south runway, where cargo flights operate. A bomb disposal robot was deployed and the detonator attached to the drone was removed. Images of the scene showed the robot close to a Ukrainian cargo plane. The US defense official told CNN the drone was carrying military-grade explosives. The same day, a second flying object hit a cargo plane near the airport, causing minor damage. The aircraft later landed safely in Hannover. Moscow accused Germany of manufacturing a “pretext” and warned it would respond to any measures. “The Russian House has long haunted them,” Maria Zakharova, spokeswoman for Russia’s foreign ministry, told CNN. “That’s why they were looking for something to latch onto. Moscow will respond to all anti-Russian decisions.” NATO chief Mark Rutte welcomed the measures announced by Germany, said the alliance’s commitment to Ukraine remained “unwavering,” and reiterated that “NATO will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend all Allies against any threat – including malign actions like those seen in Leipzig.” German media also recently reported that a third drone was found in a field near the airport about a week after incidents, prompting speculation that multiple drones were meant to be used in the attack. The German Federal Prosecutor’s Office, which is handling the case, declined to comment when contacted by CNN, citing an ongoing investigation. Leipzig/Halle, one of the busiest cargo airports in Europe, has been the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines cargo airline since Russia destroyed its home base in the town of Hostomel, northwest of Kyiv, in the early days of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The explosives-laden drone was found near one of the Ukrainian aircraft at the airport. Dobrindt said at the time that the incident represented a serious escalation. “Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past. That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario,” he said. Hybrid warfare Western intelligence services have repeatedly pointed fingers at Russia over a series of seemingly unrelated security incidents across Europe. These have included arson, high-profile hacks, GPS jamming as well as sabotage actions against key infrastructure, including undersea communication cables, logistics centers and railways. The US has warned that Russia might escalate further. Recent US intelligence assessments indicate Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve by launching a limited attack on an allied country within the next few years, according to three sources familiar with those reports. CNN contacted the Kremlin for comment on the US intel assessment on Putin as well as the assessment on the drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

articles.title: America’s expats are still waiting for tax reform
articles.summary: The United States is nearly alone in the world in taxing people based on citizenship rather than residence.
articles.body:
The U.S. is nearly alone in the world in taxing people based on citizenship rather than residence. An American who moves to Toronto, marries a Canadian citizen, raises a family there, works for a Canadian company and pays Canadian taxes will still spend decades filing annual returns with the IRS.

This is a strange way to run a tax system. And with middle-class Americans finding it difficult to find banks abroad, navigating separate tax systems and renouncing their citizenship, the practice is increasingly difficult to defend.

Last year, Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.) introduced legislation offering a sensible alternative. The Residence-Based Taxation for Americans Abroad Act would allow Americans who genuinely live overseas to select a “nonresident” tax status. They would continue paying U.S. taxes on U.S.-source income, such as rent from American property, income from a U.S. business and similar earnings. But income earned abroad would generally be taxed where it was earned.

In other words, the U.S. would begin treating Americans abroad more like every other developed country treats its citizens.

The legislation expired at the end of the 118th Congress and has yet to be formally reintroduced. LaHood and Sen. Todd Young (R-Ind.) have reportedly been working on an updated version, but progress has been slowed in part by the challenge of obtaining a revenue estimate from the Joint Committee on Taxation.

Now that Congress has returned from recess, it should prioritize finishing that work and bringing residence-based taxation back to the table, ideally as part of the next reconciliation package.

The case for reform begins with a basic principle: Taxes should generally follow economic activity. If an American lives in Germany, works in Germany and consumes German public services, Germany has the strongest claim to tax that person’s labor income. The American passport in his desk drawer should not create a second layer of tax administration thousands of miles away.

Current law provides some protection against actual double taxation through the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion and Foreign Tax Credit . But avoiding two tax bills is not the same thing as avoiding two tax systems.

Americans living abroad still need to navigate complicated filing requirements involving foreign income, bank accounts, retirement plans, corporations and investments. The Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act adds another layer by requiring foreign financial institutions to identify and report American customers. Predictably, some foreign banks simply decide American clients are not worth the compliance burden.

This turns ordinary financial activities into bureaucratic nightmares. Opening an investment account, saving for retirement or owning a small foreign business can become far more complicated simply because someone happens to hold a U.S. passport.

These burdens are not confined to wealthy Americans sheltering fortunes in Switzerland. In fact, IRS data show that most people renouncing their citizenship in recent years have moderate income levels, and about two-thirds have a net worth below $1 million. The burden falls heaviest on teachers, engineers, entrepreneurs and dual citizens who have built ordinary lives abroad.

There is also a strong self-interested economic case for reform. Americans abroad can be valuable conduits for U.S. business, investment and trade. Citizenship-based taxation makes Americans unusually costly employees overseas and can discourage internationally mobile workers from maintaining ties to the U.S.

The government already recognizes a version of this problem with corporations. The 2017 tax reforms moved the U.S. away from attempting to impose full domestic taxation on corporate profits earned around the world. Reformers understood that putting American firms at a permanent disadvantage overseas was self-defeating. American workers deserve the same consideration.

Residence-based taxation would not affect taxation of Americans living in America. U.S. residents would continue paying U.S. taxes on their worldwide income. Nor would Americans abroad suddenly receive a free pass on income generated inside the U.S. The reform would simply draw a more reasonable line between residents and nonresidents.

President Trump recognized the problem during the 2024 campaign and endorsed ending the double taxation of Americans overseas. Congress now has an opportunity to convert that promise into actual tax policy.

With lawmakers back in Washington, residence-based taxation should be on the agenda. The reconciliation is the vehicle Congress uses to make consequential changes to the tax code, and this reform certainly qualifies. After years of discussion, Americans living abroad should not have to hope that another standalone bill and another Congress will deliver.

Americans deserve treatment closer to the international norm. It is time for the U.S. to catch up.

Jack Salmon is a Gibbs Scholar and research fellow at the Mercatus Center at George Mason University.

articles.title: Germany accuses Russia of drone attack on Leipzig airport
articles.summary: This is a breaking news story.
articles.body:
The German government has accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack on a major regional airport.

Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on Tuesday afternoon that the attempted attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport in the east of the country last month, using a drone laden with explosives, fits a known pattern of “Russian hybrid operations”.

Several European countries that are providing Ukraine with support as it defends itself against Moscow’s invasion have reported an increase in sabotage attacks and attempts that they blame on Russia.

Berlin has summoned the Russian ambassador and announced diplomatic measures, while the European Union and NATO have pledged support.

The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on the evening of August 4 and defused. Berlin has concluded that “Russia is responsible for the hybrid attack in Leipzig on August 4,″ Dobrindt said.
